about: The words of the chain saga_england_south_east, THE NINE SHIPS (Data/encounters/chain_saga_england_south_east_793.json; Design/content/chains/saga_england_south_east.md): the south-east in the years when the heathen men first wintered on Thanet, 850 to 853, told at Sarre, Fordwic, Dofras, Lundenwic, Hamwic, Gipeswic and Dommoc. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the four news items the cards post; one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture and one 'art.chain_saga_england_south_east.ending.<name>' line for each ending. People: Ealdorman Ealhhere (places/sarre.json, sarre.ealhhere), King Aethelstan of Kent, Huda of Surrey, Archbishop Ceolnoth and Bishop Aethelwald of Dommoc are historical; Ceolmund is the host of places/lundenwic.json; Ketil, Beornwynn, Wihtgar, Folcbald, Wigbeorht and Osferth are ordinary invented people. Quoted from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, tr. J. Ingram, 1823: in s06.title and news.nine_ships 'fought in their ships' and 'taking nine ships and dispersing the rest' (annal 851); in s05.kingsman_aclea 'the greatest slaughter of the heathen army that we have ever heard reported to this present day' (annal 851); in end_fallen.title and news.thanet 'slain and drowned on either hand' (annal 853). 'A fleet is only men who cannot swim, standing on wood' is the ealdorman's saying in places/sarre.json. Everything else is our own wording. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Whom do you mean to sell to
The toll man does not ask what you carry. He asks whom you mean to sell to. A big man in a red cloak and a mail shirt stands behind him and listens to the answer more closely than the toll man does.
I used to ask what was in the hold. Now I am to ask where it is going. So: whom do you mean to sell to?
They have not gone home. Martinmas is past and their ships are still drawn up on the island. No army has sat a winter in this country before. This one has built huts.
A man who stays the winter must eat the winter. Thanet is good land, but it is not that good. Somebody is going to feed them, and I would like to meet him first.
That is corn in your hold. Corn goes to the strand, in daylight, to people with hearths. I say it once and pleasantly.
From the height here you see every sail that goes into the strait or past it. My watchman sees them too. He cannot tell me what they are.
You are a Frisian. You have seen their ships closer than I have, and lived. Come up at first light and count for me. Count, do not guess.
Go up at first light and count sails for him
Say you sell on the strand, in daylight, where the toll man can see
Ask what an army on an island pays for bread

You stand in the wind beside a shivering watchman and call them as they show: that one a trader, deep and slow; those three not. Forty-one hulls on the island's shore. The ealdorman cuts the number on a stick himself and gives you twenty pennies, and the toll man takes half toll of you for a month.
The toll man cuts his notch. The ealdorman nods, as a man nods at an answer he will check later. Nothing else is asked of you today.

The toll man looks at the ground. The ealdorman looks at you for some time and then says that he would not know, and that he means to. On the strand they tell you without being asked: corn is half as dear again on this water since the huts went up.
The creek and the tide

At dusk a man wades out over the saltings to your boat, up to the thigh, holding a small folding balance above the water. He speaks English like a Dane, slowly and without wasting any. He names a creek and a tide.
I am Ketil. I buy. The others do the other thing. It is cold in this water, so I will be short.
Corn. Ale if you have it. Three times what the strand gives you. I know what the strand gives you. I asked.
Silver by weight, on this balance, and you may bring your own weights and laugh at mine. I cut it where you can see the inside.
You were on the down this morning, counting us. Good. A man who can count is a man I can pay. Men on downs get hungry too.
They say at the toll post that a Frisian asked what we pay. It is not a secret. I am pleased somebody asked.
The creek behind the long bank, east of the crossing. Come in on the top of the night tide, no light. If the ealdorman's man is there instead of me, I was never here.
Take his order: six sacks of wheat to the creek within the month
Hear him out, then give the ealdorman's man the creek and the tide
Say your corn is spoken for, and wish him a dry walk home

He weighs out thirty pennies' worth of cut silver in earnest, an arm ring in four pieces, and wades back the way he came. Six sacks, the creek, within the month. A dog barks somewhere on the Kent shore, and you do not know whose dog.

The reeve's man hears it twice and gives you twenty-five pennies. Three nights later there are spears in the reeds behind the long bank, and nobody comes to the creek. Ketil is not a fool. He will have worked out who knew.

He shrugs with the balance still held up. Going, he lets fall that there are more than forty crews in the huts, that they have salted Thanet's cattle already, and that more ships are looked for in spring. All three are true.
The sisters on the island

At the abbess's ship-house a nun stands over four roped chests and six girls in travelling cloaks too big for them. The minster's own ship lies on her side in the shed, dry and tight, with no one to sail her.
I am Beornwynn, of Saint Mildrith's minster. You know where our minster is. It is on the same island as they are, an hour's walk from their huts.
They have not touched us. They came once, very civil, and counted our cattle. Our abbess says a man does not count what he means to leave.

In our grandmothers' day the sisters of Lyminge were given a house inside Canterbury's wall, for a refuge. The archbishop says there is room in it. So: the books, the altar silver, and the six youngest.
The rest of us stay. Saint Mildrith is not going anywhere, so neither are we. She has seen off worse than Danes. She saw off an abbess once.
We have a ship. The old king freed her of toll here and at Fordwic. Her master went to the ealdorman's levy and her crew with him. A ship is a great comfort in a shed.
People see boats at night on this water. I see them too. I say my prayers and I do not ask whose. Today I am asking only about chests.
Carry the sister, the girls and the chests up the Stour to Fordwic
Give silver for a cart and oxen, and wish her the road
Say the boat is laden, and tell her which tide is safest for the ferry

Four chests amidships, six girls on them, and a nun in the bow who has opinions about your steering. She pays ninety pennies from the abbess's chest before you cast off, so that it is carriage and not charity. The girls ask riddles the whole way up the Stour. You are given one to keep.
Fifteen pennies hires a cart and two oxen at the ferry. They go by the road, which is longer and has no tide in it. She blesses you briefly, like a woman with a cart to load.
You tell her to cross at the last of the flood, when the ferry runs straight and nobody can wade after it. She thanks you for that, and goes to find the ferryman.
An open beach
The Strand is as open as it ever was: no bank, no ditch, booths down to the tide line. Your host wants to know what is on Thanet. The king's reeve wants to know why it should be his trouble.
Nine years ago I stood in that river to my chest with nine people and watched this beach burn. I know what a sail is. Tell me what you saw in the strait.
Huts? They built huts? Then they are not going home to sow. So where do forty crews go in spring, when the island is eaten?
Thanet is in Kent. Kent is the West Saxon's. This is King Beorhtwulf's town. I do not see that a Kentish island is a Mercian reeve's affair.
The ealdorman of Kent sends me a count by a Frisian. Well. How many keels? Say it again, slower.
A ditch across the roads, your host says. A ditch costs a hundred men a month. I have asked the king. The king is thinking about the Welsh.
I keep a spear inside the door now. My grandfather kept a tally stick there. Each of us keeps what he expects to need.
Tell Ceolmund what a wintered fleet does in spring, and help him bury the yard's silver and weights
Give the reeve the ealdorman's count, keel by keel
Sell what you brought and say it is not your beach

You tell him plainly: a fleet that has wintered is rested, hungry and close, and this is the richest open beach it can reach in two tides. That night you lift the hearthstones together. The yard's silver, the lead weights and the bronze balance go under, and his wife's kin are sent over the river before Easter.
Forty-one on the shore, and room cleared for more. The reeve gives you thirty pennies and half toll for two months, and writes nothing down. A count that is written has to be answered.
You sell. Ceolmund says nothing against it; a guest is a guest. A woolman tells you corn is a third dearer than last spring, because none is coming up from Kent, and nobody on the Strand asks why.
Ships wanted
A king's thegn with a new scar and a shipwright with tar to the elbows are going along the shore asking every master the same two things: what he has in his hold, and how well he knows the Wantsum.
You have not heard? Three hundred and fifty ships in the Thames mouth. They broke Canterbury. They broke London, and the Mercian king ran. Then they came over the river into Surrey.
King Aethelwulf met them at Aclea with his son. I was there. It was the greatest slaughter of the heathen army that we have ever heard reported to this present day. And there are still ships.
Wihtgar, from the Dour. I build boats at Dofras. I came here for tar and for hulls, because the king's father has a yard here and nobody left in the town to use it.
Wihtgar. This is my ground. I have built fishing boats on it for twenty years and now I am asked for ships to fight from. I said: the same thing, longer, and God help whoever stands in it.
A man came down from the Strand with nothing but his children. He said a Frisian made him bury his weights before Easter. The yard burned. The weights did not. Was that you?
King Aethelstan means to meet them on the water when they go home laden, in the south mouth by the sand landing. Nobody has done it. We need tar, and a man who knows that bar.
Say you know the south mouth, and will bring the king's ships in through it
Take the wright's order for tar
Tell them what you saw on the strait, and go about your trade

The thegn counts forty pennies into your hand as earnest and tells you to be on the Wantsum about Michaelmas. Wihtgar asks how much water there is on the bar at half ebb. You tell him. He says that is less than he hoped and more than he feared.
Four barrels of tar inside forty days, at four-fifths over the price. Wihtgar spits on his hand and holds it out. He says a ship built in a hurry is mostly tar anyway.

You tell them of the huts, the count, and the creek behind the long bank. The thegn thanks you. The wright tells you, as one tradesman to another, that every yard from here to the Dour wants tar and will pay well over the odds for it.
They fought in their ships

Word runs down the strait that the fleet is coming home out of the Thames, low in the water with Canterbury's goods. In the south mouth, off the sand landing, the king's ships lie with their masts down. Nobody in Kent has done this before, and everybody in Kent has come to watch.
The men are afraid of the water, not the Danes. I told them: a fleet is only men who cannot swim, standing on wood. They said: so are we. Which is true.
My father beat them on land. My brother stood beside him. I have a strait and some green ships, and I mean to be the first of us to beat them where they live.
That is your tar on every seam of them. If they leak, I shall say so to the king, and name you. They will not leak.
Green oak and not enough tar. They will float for a day. I have told the king a day is what he has.
You said you knew this bar. The king's steersmen know rivers. Take the first ship's oar and the rest will follow your stern. I will be standing behind you, so do not turn round quickly.
One thing first. I have a corn sack out of a creek, tied with a knot my reeve calls Frisian. I am busy today. I will be less busy this winter.
They will come on the ebb, heavy, with the sun in their eyes. Where will you be?
Take the steering oar of the first ship and bring them out on the ebb
Stand on the down with the watchman and call the sails as they come
Lie up the Stour until it is over

You take them out over the bar on the last of the ebb with a hand's breadth under the keel, and the laden ships cannot turn. It is short, loud and close. Nine are taken and the rest row for the open sea. The king gives you two hundred and twenty pennies and the ealdorman three bundles of spearheads out of a prize, and says he asked for the second ship and got the fourth.

Your ship touches the bar and hangs there while the others go round you; your shoulder meets the oar loom and loses. They take nine all the same, and the rest row for the open sea. The king gives you a hundred and twenty pennies. The ealdorman says a man who goes aground first has at least gone first.

You call them from the down: sixteen, low, in two lines, the big one third. A boy runs each word down the hill. By evening nine of them are on the sand with English spears in them and the rest are small on the sea. The ealdorman pays you ninety pennies from his own purse and says the watchman can keep his eyes for sheep.

You hear it from up the river as a noise like a fair a long way off. By night the news comes with the tide: nine ships taken, the rest fled. At the hythe they tell you corn is very dear in Canterbury, where the roofs are off and the barns are ash.
A book without its boards

Among hones and combs on a Frisian's cloth lies a book with bare oak boards, the nail holes still bright where a cover was torn off. A priest stands looking at it with his hands behind his back, as a man looks at a horse he cannot afford.
Folcbald, of Dorestad. I buy what the fleet cannot use. They kept the silver off the front. This is the part that was left over. Calfskin, a hundred and sixty leaves, hardly wet.
A hundred and twenty pennies. I gave a Dane a cask of ale for it, so you see I am an honest man: I tell you my profit to your face.
It is a psalter. That is a Canterbury hand, the old good one, not what they write now. Somebody wrote 'pray for Eadhun' at the foot of a leaf. I have been praying for him all morning.

Bishop Aethelwald swore his obedience to the archbishop in writing. He would buy this back for Canterbury today, if the see of Dommoc had a hundred and twenty pennies. It has a cliff and a great many gulls.
Saint Peter's has a wooden cup and a debt to the thatcher. I have offered him forty pennies and a mass every year for ever. He says he has no use for the mass, being a careful man and seldom at sea.
If no churchman buys it by the herring, the leaves go to a man who makes drum skins and book covers. Parchment is parchment. I did not burn Canterbury. I only keep a stall.
Pay his price and take the book for Canterbury
Say bare boards are firewood, and beat him down
Tell the priest whose book it is, and leave it to the Church

A hundred and twenty pennies, counted twice. The priest wraps the book in his own cloak for you and reads you the first psalm from it before he lets go, pointing at each word. You find you know three of them afterwards.
You tell him what oak boards fetch as kindling and what a Frisian's name fetches in Kent this year. He takes seventy pennies and says you drive a hard bargain for a man buying the word of God.
He lets you talk, and then begins to fold the cloth with the book in it. You pay the hundred and twenty. He says next time it will be a hundred and thirty, for the conversation.

You tell the priest it is Canterbury's, and that Canterbury would want to know. He says he will send word south by the next monk who is walking that way. The book stays on the cloth, between the hones and the combs.
Inside the wall

The landing below Canterbury smells of new thatch and old smoke. The archbishop's clerk is at the hythe with a list of what was taken, and the ealdorman is there too, on his way through, in no hurry to leave a merchant he knows.
Wigbeorht, Archbishop Ceolnoth's clerk. This is the list of what they took from Christ Church. It is longer than the list of what we have. I meet every boat, in case.
That is our psalter. That is Eadhun's hand; he taught the man who taught me. Where did you find it? No. First tell me what you want for it. I would rather hear the worst at once.
The six from Thanet are in the refuge and have learned the long psalms. Sister Beornwynn went back to the island by the next ferry. She said she had left bread rising.
We took nine ships. The king had the best, God keep him, we have not seen him since the autumn. I asked for the second and got the fourth. I keep her on the Stour and look at her.
Now. The sack with the knot. I know the creek, I know the tide, and I think I know the boat. I would rather be told than find out. It is cheaper for everyone.
They are still on the island. Next summer, after the hay, I go over and end it. Huda is bringing the men of Surrey. With his and mine it can be done between two tides.
Hear me, as a friend. Stay off the strait that day. Men who cannot swim will be crossing water in a hurry, and a merchant's boat is the first thing they will climb into.
Lay the psalter on Christ's altar and name no price
Name what you paid and a fair profit on it
Tell the ealdorman about the creek yourself, pay the fine and swear off the camp
Eat the hythe's bread and listen

You carry it up the track and lay it on the altar yourself. The clerk cannot speak for a while. The archbishop sends down a hundred and fifty pennies all the same, because a church that takes gifts from merchants and gives none back gets no more. The writing room gives you a riddle about a thief who ate words, and an afternoon of letters.
You name the price. The clerk counts two hundred and forty pennies out of three different bags, slowly, and writes it on his list in a small hand. He thanks you correctly.

You tell it: the creek, the tide, six sacks. The ealdorman hears it out, names sixty pennies, and has you swear on the hythe's cross to sell the island nothing more. Then he says that a man who tells him to his face may lie where he likes on the day, and he will not ask why.
The bread is new and the ale is thin. You learn that Canterbury will buy oak for a year at nearly half over the price, and that the ealdorman does not make the same request twice.
How wide is that water

There are ditches across the roads of the wic now, a man deep. At Ceolmund's yard a young ealdorman from over the river is buying ale by the cartload and asking Frisians about a strait he has never seen.
We have our ditch. The king found the hundred men the summer after he ran. It is a good ditch. It would have been a better one two years ago.
The house burned over them and they were still there under the hearth, weights, balance and all. I weigh with them every day. You do not pay for a bed in this yard again, nor your sons.
They took the weights, the balance and my wife's brother. I bought new weights. The reeve says they are honest. They feel light to me.
Huda, of Surrey. That fleet walked through my shire on its way to be beaten at Aclea. It took its time. I have barns that are still black.
After the hay I take my men into Kent. Ealhhere and I go over to that island together. He says it can be done between two tides. He is older than I am, so I believe him.
You sail that strait. My men are ploughmen. They have forded the Wey and think they know water. Tell me truly: how wide is it, and what does it do?
Tell him how the Wantsum runs: when the ford bares, and how fast it comes back
Take his order for ale for the march
Wish him luck, and ask Ceolmund what sells

You draw it in spilt ale on the board. Two places only where a man can cross. The ford bares for about as long as a mass and a meal. Then it comes back from both ends at once, quicker than a man walks in mail, and the mud holds his feet while it comes. He has you say it again to his captains. He pays for the ale, twenty pennies, though you drank none of it.
Six casks to this yard inside forty days, at three-fifths over the price. Huda says ploughmen march on ale and fight on the memory of it.
He thanks you for the luck as a man does who has asked for something else. Ceolmund tells you ale is a third dearer in the wic since the levy began to gather, and will be until it marches.
At the ebb
The landing is full of men and no goods. Kent and Surrey are going over to the island when the ford bares. The ferryman has drawn his boat up on the chalk and is watching the water, not the men.
They go at the ebb. The ford gives them the space of a mass and a meal, and then it is a strait again. I have told the ealdorman. He said he would be quick.
I told you to stay off this water today. You are a hard man to keep away from a market. There is nothing to buy.
Well. If you will not go, lie at the ford's end with that boat and keep her afloat. I do not order it. I do not expect to need it. I would like to know it is there.
I have told every man of mine what you drew on that board. When they hear the horn they turn and go back, winning or not. Whether they will do it is another thing.
It is less than I thought. You could throw a spear across. My men have forded worse in a wet spring.
If they are still fighting when it turns, the water will not wait for the better side. Do not be on it in a small boat unless you mean to be.
Lie at the ford's end with the boat through the whole tide, and take off whoever comes
Lie under the minster's shore instead, for the sisters who stayed and the hurt
Go round to the creek on the same tide: whoever wins will want bread
Stay off the strait, as he said

At first they have the better of it; you hear that from the shouting. Then the water turns. The horn sounds and the men of Surrey come back in a body, as they were told, and the Kentishmen behind them, and the tide takes the slow and the Danes who follow. You take men off the mud until the boat has a hand of freeboard. The last is a big man in a red cloak with a broken leg, swearing steadily. Huda is not among them.

At first they have the better of it. Then the water turns, and nobody turns with it. They are still fighting on the far bank when the ford closes behind them, and after that there are men in the water on either hand, in mail, and the mud has their feet. You take off the ones you can reach. Late in the tide you bring the ealdorman over, under his own red cloak. A boy says Huda lies on the other side.

You lie in the minster's creek with the sail down. Before dark the hurt begin to come over the fields, Kent and Surrey together, and the sisters carry them down on hurdles. You cross six times that night. Sister Beornwynn holds the lantern low and counts every head aboard, every time, like loaves.

You go round by the north mouth while every eye in Kent is on the ford. Ketil is at the creek before you, calm as a toll man. Behind him the camp is burning at one end and cheering at the other. He weighs out sixty pennies of cut silver and says the bread will be wanted more tomorrow, whoever is left to eat it.
You lie up the Stour, as he asked. The noise comes over the marsh for half a day and then stops. The news comes after it by the ferry, a man at a time.
Slain and drowned on either hand
The ferry has been carrying back what the water gave up. A grey steward waits at the landing with something wrapped in a red cloak, and asks for the Frisian by name.
At first they were winning. Everybody says that, and it is true. Then it turned. I have fetched over ninety-four so far. I do not sort them. The water did not.
Osferth, steward to Ealdorman Ealhhere, who is dead, and Huda of Surrey with him. The heathen men are still on the island. I say it in that order because that is how it was told to me.
It was your boat that brought him over. The lady knows it. She asked whose, and the ferryman said the Frisian's, and she said: then he is not to wait at any door of ours.
You were not on the strait that day. He asked you not to be. He said the Frisian was the one man in Kent who did what he was told, and laughed. It was the morning of the fight.
There is a corn sack in his hall with a knot in it. He never said whose. I burned it yesterday. I am a steward, not a reeve, and I have enough to bury.
His sister Ealhburh sends you this, which he drank from, and silver. His brother will be ealdorman. He says what Ealhhere promised stands. Which will you have?
Take the gilded cup his sister sends
Ask instead for what he promised: a keel free of toll at Sarre
Say only that you brought him over, and ask nothing
Seven hundred pennies, and the cup: silver, gilded inside, dented at the lip where it hung from a saddle. The steward says it holds more than it looks, like the man. Your house keeps it.

Six hundred pennies, and the new ealdorman's word given at the toll post before witnesses: one keel of yours pays no toll at Sarre while he lives. The toll man cuts a notch of a new shape and shows it you, so that you will know it again.

You say you brought him over and that it is not a thing a man is paid for. The steward goes away and comes back with the lady's answer: eleven hundred pennies, the cup, and the freedom of the toll, and a message that she does not argue with merchants about what things are worth.
The fourth ship
The ealdorman sits on an upturned boat with one leg bound to a spar, drinking from a gilded cup. Drawn up beside him is a long Danish hull, newly tarred, with a shipwright under her counting rivets.
I have said for years that a fleet is only men who cannot swim, standing on wood. I can now add that an army is the same, without the wood. Sit down.
Huda is dead. He turned his men when the horn blew and went back himself for the ones who did not hear it. Surrey came home because of him. Kent came home because of a Frisian with a boat.
Wihtgar. We have met. She is sound: Danish oak, sixteen oars, new rivets where I did not like theirs. I have tarred her twice. She will take six times what your boat takes, and go to windward of it.
That is the fourth of the nine. I asked for the second, you remember. I have looked at her for two years and never once been to sea in her. I am told I am not to go to sea again.
One thing you should know. They are still on the island, and they saw whose sail lay at the ford. They are careful men. They will know it again.
I owe you a leg and whatever goes with it. I am the king's ealdorman in Kent and I have forty hides at Lenham. Ask, and do not be modest. It wastes my time.
Take the fourth ship
Ask ground above the tide here, and a keel free of toll
Say a boat was at a ford, and ask only that his toll men know your sail

He has her run down into the water there and then, and twelve hundred pennies put aboard for her first lading. Wihtgar walks her length once more and hands you a bag of spare rivets. The ealdorman says that in every port of Kent you are now his friend, and that it is a thing with uses.

A plot above the tide at Sarre, paced out by the reeve with the ealdorman watching from his boat; one keel free of the toll here; and fifteen hundred pennies to build on it. He says ground is a sensible thing to ask for by a man who nearly ran out of it.

He looks at you for some time. Then he sends for two thousand pennies anyway, tells the toll man that your keel pays nothing at Sarre, and says before his riders that the Frisian is his friend. He says he will decide what his own leg is worth.
Cut honestly
Ketil does not wade any more. He comes along the shore in daylight with two men and a leather bag. Nobody at the toll post looks up, which is its own kind of looking.
You came on the day itself. I did not think you would. The others say you have a cold heart. I said: no, he has a full hold. It is not the same.
Both their big men are dead. So are a good many of ours; it was not a cheap day. Nobody on your side will write that part down.
We will not sit on this island for ever. There is another, in the mouth of the big river, with sheep on it. Somebody will have to buy for that winter too.
This stick has our notches on it. Show it from your bow and ships of this fleet will look at something else. It does not work on other fleets. I am an honest man.
I have a boat of my own now and no wish to die in a hut. Put your purse beside mine. Or take the bag and go. Either is a fair bargain. The toll man is watching you choose.
Lay your purse beside his and call it one
Take the bag by weight, and no oath
Take what you are owed, and tell him it was the last sack

Two purses on one cloak, and an oath on his arm ring and your cross, each man looking politely away from the other's. Nine hundred pennies is your half. Ketil will sail his own boat where you send it and share what it makes. The toll man has seen all of it, and so by tomorrow has Kent.

Eighteen hundred pennies by weight, in arm rings, cut dirhams and the foot of a chalice you do not look at closely. He cuts where you can see the inside. He gives you the stick as well. At the toll post nothing is said, and nothing will be forgotten.

You take the six hundred you are owed and tell him the creek is shut. He nods, and lets you keep the stick: a bargain is a bargain. It makes no difference at the toll post. Somebody saw the boat three winters ago.
The ship in the shed

The doors of the abbess's ship-house stand open for the first time in three years. The minster's ship has been turned upright and scraped, and the abbess herself has come over the water to see who is to have her.
Six crossings. Seventy-one living, and four who were not by the time we landed. I counted. Somebody had to, and you were steering.
Both ealdormen are dead and the heathen men are still an hour from my gate. I have buried Kentishmen and Surrey men in one row. The saint has not objected.
We stay. We have always stayed. But a house that stays needs someone who goes: to Fordwic, to the wic at London, for salt and wax and news. Our master is under the row I spoke of.
She is free of toll here and at Fordwic by the old king's writing. What she earns is shown to us first. It is a fair rule and I shall enforce it.
I am told merchants like to name their own price, and I like to hear a price before I pray over it. What will you have of Saint Mildrith?
Take the steering oar of the minster's ship, under her freedom of toll
Ask a bay in the ship-house, and a place in the sisters' book of names
Ask the carriage money for a night's work, and no more

She goes down the hard on rollers with six nuns hauling and Sister Beornwynn giving the time. Six hundred pennies for her first lading. You are her master: she pays no toll at Sarre or at Fordwic, and what she carries is shown to the minster first. The abbess says the saint has had worse shipmen.

A bay in the ship-house with your mark on the post, eight hundred pennies, and your name written in the book the sisters read from at the altar. The abbess gives you a folded strip of linen that lay a year on Saint Mildrith's tomb, and tells you to keep it dry and not to sell it.

You ask a night's carriage. The abbess says she knows the price of a night's carriage and this was not that night. A thousand pennies, and one keel of your own free of toll at Sarre: she has the old king's writing, and she can lend a line of it.
This winter the heathen men did not go home. More than forty crews sit in huts on Thanet, and more ships are looked for in spring.

This year three hundred and fifty ships came into the mouth of the Thames. Canterbury and London were stormed and the king of the Mercians put to flight. King Aethelwulf and his son beat the army at Aclea.
This year King Aethelstan and Ealdorman Ealhhere fought in their ships at Sandwich in Kent, taking nine ships and dispersing the rest.
This year Ealhhere with the men of Kent and Huda with the men of Surrey fought the heathen army on Thanet, and at first had the victory. Many men were slain and drowned on either hand.

A grey winter morning at a toll post on a chalk shore: a toll man with a tally stick looking at the viewer, and behind his shoulder a big sandy-bearded man in a red cloak over mail; far across flat water, a low island with thin smoke rising from a row of huts and dark hulls drawn up below them.

Dusk on the saltings, the tide half in, a red band under low cloud: a broad Dane wading thigh-deep toward a small boat, one arm held high with a little folding balance in it; reeds and a long mud bank behind him, no other person in sight.

A cold bright noon at an open boat shed on a chalk hard: a nun of about forty in a dark veil standing over four roped chests, six girls in cloaks too long for them sitting in a row on the chests; behind them in the shed a small clinker ship lying on her side.

A windy spring afternoon on the Strand at London: booths and beached hulls down to the tide line, no wall or ditch anywhere; in front a spare man with a burn scar on his forearm and a spear leaning by his door, talking to a merchant, while a well-dressed reeve stands a little apart looking down the river.

A hot late-summer day on a half-empty shore, grass growing between old house plots: a thegn with a fresh scar across his cheek and a shipwright tarred to the elbows walking along a line of beached boats; behind them a long new hull in frame, ribs bare, and a tar pot smoking.

Early morning, the sun low and behind the viewer, at the sandy south mouth of the strait: English ships with masts lowered and crowded with spearmen pushing out over a bar on the ebb; beyond them a line of laden Danish ships, low in the water, square sails just filling; people watching from a chalk down on the left.

An autumn market on a hurdle bank under a grey sky: a Frisian trader's cloth spread with whetstones and bone combs, and among them a thick book with bare oak boards and bright nail holes; a thin priest stooping over it with his hands behind his back, herring boats beached behind.

A mild day at a river hythe below a walled city with new pale thatch among burnt roofs: a clerk with a long list on a strip of parchment meeting a boat at the water's edge; behind him the big red-cloaked ealdorman sitting his horse at ease, a gilded cup hanging from the saddle.

Evening in a fenced yard at London, a fresh deep ditch cutting the road outside the gate: a young lord in a blue cloak leaning over a board on which a merchant draws a strait in spilt ale; the spare scarred host standing behind with a jug, carts loaded with ale casks at the fence.

A still summer noon at the crossing: hundreds of spearmen wading out over bared mud and shallow water toward a low island with smoke on it, the red-cloaked ealdorman and a young lord in blue at their head; in front a ferryman sitting on his drawn-up boat watching the water's edge, and one small merchant boat afloat at the ford's end.

A grey wet evening at the landing: a ferry boat coming in low with covered shapes in it; on the chalk a grey-haired steward holding a bundle wrapped in a red cloak, the rim of a gilded cup showing; the tide full and flat behind, the island dark.

A bright morning on the hard: the big ealdorman sitting on an upturned boat, one leg splinted to a spar, raising a gilded cup; beside him a long, newly tarred Danish hull on rollers with a shipwright crouched under her; the strait blue and empty behind.

Plain daylight on the shore below the toll post: a broad Dane and two men walking up openly with a leather bag, a notched stick in the Dane's other hand; in the background the toll man at his bench with his head carefully turned away; long ships on the far shore.

A clear morning at the ship-house with its doors wide open: a small clinker ship upright on rollers at the head of the hard, nuns at the ropes, an old abbess with a staff and the cellaress Beornwynn standing by her stem; over the water the island and the minster's two church roofs.
A gilded silver cup, dented at the lip, standing on a merchant's sea chest beside a tally stick with one notch of a strange shape; through the open door behind, the strait at full tide.

A long Danish ship under an English merchant's striped sail standing out of the Wantsum's south mouth past a sand landing; on the down above, a man with a stick and a bound leg, in a red cloak, watching her go.
Two boats lying side by side in a reed creek at dawn, one Frisian, one Danish; two purses on one cloak across the thwarts between them; far off on the Kent shore, a small figure on a horse, watching.

The minster's small ship going up a marsh river under a square sail with a cross sewn on it, a nun in the bow, salt sacks and wax amidships; a toll man on the bank lifting his hand to wave her through.
